entities.name: Jail
entities.intro: Prison, which satyagrahis court deliberately. Gandhi's first term was in 1908.

entities.name: Tolstoy Farm
entities.intro: A farm 21 miles from Johannesburg, given by Kallenbach, where satyagrahi families lived together during the struggle.

entities.name: Pragji Desai
entities.intro: A satyagrahi who helped teach at Tolstoy Farm.

entities.name: The unruly youth
entities.intro: A wild, quarrelsome 17-year-old at Tolstoy Farm.

entities.name: Sorabji Adajania
entities.intro: Gandhi's jail comrade and one of the best satyagrahis, sent to London to qualify as a barrister.

entities.name: Dr. Jivraj Mehta
entities.intro: An Indian doctor in London who treated Gandhi.

entities.name: Lord Crewe
entities.intro: Secretary of State for India in 1914.

entities.name: Sarojini Naidu
entities.intro: Poet and nationalist, member of the Lyceum ladies' club in London.

entities.name: Emily Hobhouse
entities.intro: English campaigner who exposed the Boer War concentration camps.

entities.name: World War I
entities.intro: The war declared on 4 August 1914, two days before Gandhi reached London.

entities.name: Hind Swaraj
entities.intro: Gandhi's 1909 booklet on Indian home rule and modern civilization.

chapters.situation: Kasturbai has recovered at Phoenix after refusing beef tea. Gandhi has now been to jail for the first time, in 1908.
chapters.summary: Gandhi finds some jail rules, such as no tea and the last meal before sunset, are good disciplines for a brahmachari, and adopts them voluntarily after his release. When Kasturbai's bleeding returns, he begs her to give up salt and pulses. She challenges him to give them up himself, and he vows on the spot to abstain for a year. Shocked, she begs him to retract it and agrees to give them up herself, but he refuses. She recovers quickly, and Gandhi keeps the abstinence for ten years, calling it 'one of the sweetest recollections of my life'.

updates.gandhi: First jailed in 1908. Gives up tea and eats nothing after sunset. Vows to give up salt and pulses to support Kasturbai, and keeps it for ten years.
updates.kasturba: Dares her husband to give up salt and pulses, then begs him to take back his vow when he does. She gives them up herself and recovers.
updates.jail: First imprisonment, 1908. The no-tea, meal-before-sunset rules become Gandhi's own discipline.
updates.satyagraha: Gandhi calls his salt-and-pulses vow for Kasturba a 'domestic satyagraha'.
updates.diet: No salt and no pulses for ten years, and no tea.
updates.naturecure: Kasturbai's bleeding stops after the diet change, adding to Gandhi's 'reputation as a quack'.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has given up salt and pulses for Kasturbai's sake and is tightening his diet to support his brahmacharya vow.
chapters.summary: Influenced by Raychandbhai's view that milk stimulates passion, and by reports of cruelty to Calcutta's dairy cows, Gandhi and Kallenbach give up milk together at Tolstoy Farm in 1912. Kallenbach, once a lover of luxury introduced through Mr. Khan, has cut his spending from Rs. 1,200 to Rs. 120 a month and lives with Gandhi. They move to a cheap, uncooked fruit diet of groundnuts, bananas, dates, lemons and olive oil. Gandhi warns that the mind matters most, and that diet only helps.

updates.gandhi: Gives up milk with Kallenbach in 1912 and lives on raw fruit and nuts, aiming to live like the poorest.
updates.kallenbach: A former lover of luxury who cuts his expenses from Rs. 1,200 to Rs. 120 a month. Proposes giving up milk and lives with Gandhi after the household breaks up.
updates.raychand: First taught Gandhi that milk stimulates passion.
updates.diet: No milk from 1912. Raw groundnuts, bananas, dates, lemons and olive oil, with almost no cooking.
updates.brahmacharya: Diet helps, but 'mind is the principal thing'; only self-examination, surrender and grace cleanse it.
updates.tolstoyfarm: Gandhi and Kallenbach give up milk here in 1912.

chapters.situation: Gandhi and Kallenbach live on fruit at Tolstoy Farm among satyagrahi families.
chapters.summary: Gandhi begins full water-only fasts on Ekadashi for self-restraint and keeps pradosha through the month of Shravan, which coincides with Ramzan. He encourages the Muslim youngsters to keep the Ramzan fast and invites Hindus, Parsis and Christians to join in their own way. The Hindu youngsters cook vegetarian delicacies for the Muslims' sunset meals, and a strong team spirit grows. He warns that physical fasting without mental fasting ends in hypocrisy.

updates.gandhi: Fasts on water alone for self-restraint and encourages all faiths on the Farm to fast together.
updates.putlibai: Gandhi recalls copying her vows and fasts as a boy without understanding them.
updates.tolstoyfarm: Hindu, Muslim, Parsi and Christian youngsters fast side by side during Ramzan and Shravan. Everyone is vegetarian, and the Muslim boys never complain.
updates.islam: Gandhi makes sure the Muslim youths say namaz and keep Ramzan.
updates.religion: Gandhi encourages each child in their own observances and believes in joining others in self-denial.
updates.diet: Fasting is a means to self-restraint only if the mind fasts too.

chapters.situation: Tolstoy Farm has become home to satyagrahi families with children of several religions.
chapters.summary: With no money for teachers and no faith in conventional schooling, Gandhi takes on the role of father and teacher to the Farm's children, putting character first. There are no servants, so the children cook, garden, dig pits, fell timber and carry loads. Kallenbach learns shoemaking at a Trappist monastery and teaches it to Gandhi, who teaches the children, and there is a small carpentry class. The rule is that teachers always work alongside the pupils.

updates.gandhi: Becomes schoolmaster at Tolstoy Farm, learns shoemaking from Kallenbach, and works alongside the children.
updates.kallenbach: Learns shoemaking at a Trappist monastery, runs the gardening, and helps teach.
updates.pragji: Helps teach classes at Tolstoy Farm.
updates.education: Character before literacy. Children learn through manual labour and trades, with teachers working beside them.
updates.tolstoyfarm: No servants; all work from cooking to scavenging is done by the residents. Fine health, little illness.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is teaching the children at Tolstoy Farm, with physical and vocational work in the mornings.
chapters.summary: Literary classes come after lunch, when Gandhi is exhausted. Teaching each child in their own language, he struggles through Tamil and Urdu, which he barely knows, and lets the Tamil boys interpret for him. Never hiding his ignorance keeps their respect. He uses few textbooks, believing 'the true textbook for the pupil is his teacher', and teaches mostly by talking.

updates.gandhi: Teaches Hindi, Tamil, Gujarati, Urdu, Sanskrit basics and English, often half-asleep.
updates.education: Teaching in the mother tongue by word of mouth, with almost no textbooks.
updates.tamil: Gandhi teaches the Tamil script to South African-born Tamil boys, who out-talk him in conversation.
updates.truth: Gandhi never hides his ignorance from his pupils and keeps their love and respect.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is teaching the Farm's children languages and trades, but finds training their spirit the hardest part.
chapters.summary: Gandhi concludes that spiritual training cannot come from books, only from the teacher's own life, so the children become his teachers by forcing him to live straight. Once, exasperated by a violent, lying 17-year-old, he strikes him with a ruler while trembling. The youth begs forgiveness because he senses Gandhi's pain. Gandhi still repents the blow as showing 'the brute' in him and never uses corporal punishment again.

updates.gandhi: Strikes a pupil with a ruler once and repents it for life. His wards push him toward more self-discipline.
updates.wildyouth: A 17-year-old Gandhi hits with a ruler. He begs forgiveness on seeing Gandhi's distress and never disobeys him again.
updates.education: Spirit can only be trained by example: 'It would be idle for me, if I were a liar, to teach boys to tell the truth.'
updates.ahimsa: Gandhi regrets his one blow: 'I exhibited before him that day not the spirit, but the brute, in me.'

chapters.situation: Tolstoy Farm takes in all sorts of youngsters, including some unruly ones from Johannesburg.
chapters.summary: Kallenbach objects to Gandhi's own sons mixing with the Farm's unruly boys and loafers. Gandhi says he is equally responsible for all of them, that sending the others away would return them to bad ways, and that his sons must not think themselves superior. He concludes the experiment did his sons good, as long as parents keep watch.

updates.gandhi: Refuses to separate his sons from the Farm's 'bad' boys.
updates.kallenbach: Worries that mixing Gandhi's sons with unruly youths will corrupt them.
updates.manilal: Raised alongside rougher boys at Tolstoy Farm, and loses any sense of superiority.
updates.ramdas: Raised alongside rougher boys at Tolstoy Farm.
updates.devdas: Raised alongside rougher boys at Tolstoy Farm.
updates.education: Good and bad children can be taught together if parents watch closely; children kept 'in cottonwool' are not protected from temptation.

chapters.situation: Many satyagrahis have been released from jail and Tolstoy Farm is emptying, so Gandhi moves the remaining residents to Phoenix.
chapters.summary: In Johannesburg Gandhi hears of 'the moral fall' of two Phoenix residents. Kasturba had warned him earlier. Feeling responsible as their guardian, he imposes a seven-day fast and four and a half months of one meal a day; Kallenbach insists on joining. His anger turns to pity, and the penance clears the air. A later episode leads to a 14-day fast, which goes hard because he drinks too little water.

updates.gandhi: Fasts for seven days, then 14, as penance for two wards' moral lapse, taking responsibility for it himself.
updates.kasturba: Had warned Gandhi about the two wards, but he ignored her.
updates.kallenbach: Brings Gandhi the news and joins his penance.
updates.phoenix: Two residents' moral lapse leads to Gandhi's penitential fasts.
updates.diet: Fasting becomes penance. Gandhi learns he must drink plenty of water while fasting.
updates.education: 'There is no question about the teacher's responsibility for the errors of his pupil.'

chapters.situation: The satyagraha struggle in South Africa has concluded in 1914, and Gokhale has asked Gandhi to come home to India by way of London.
chapters.summary: Gandhi, Kasturba and Kallenbach sail third class to England, eating fruit and nuts. Gandhi argues with Kallenbach over his costly binoculars until, by agreement, he throws them out of the porthole. Still weak from fasting, Gandhi strains his legs walking on deck, and Dr. Jivraj Mehta orders complete rest. War is declared on 4 August, and they reach London on the 6th.

updates.gandhi: Leaves South Africa for good in July 1914. Arrives in London weak from fasting, two days after war is declared.
updates.kallenbach: Agrees to Gandhi's throwing his £7 binoculars into the sea and never regrets it.
updates.jivraj: Warns that Gandhi's legs may give out without complete rest.
updates.gokhale: Tells Gandhi to return home via London.
updates.satyagraha: The South African struggle concluded in 1914; its story is told in Gandhi's separate book.
updates.ww1: War breaks out as their ship enters the English Channel.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has reached London just as World War I breaks out, hoping to see Gokhale, who is stranded in Paris.
chapters.summary: Gandhi argues that Indians in Britain should serve the Empire in its hour of need rather than exploit it, though others say slaves should not help their masters. About 80 volunteers train in first aid under Dr. Cantlie, and Lord Crewe accepts their offer of service. Gandhi meets Sarojini Naidu for the first time when she hands him clothes to sew for soldiers.

updates.gandhi: Organizes an Indian ambulance volunteer corps in London and trains in first aid.
updates.gokhale: Stranded in Paris by the war.
updates.sorabji: In London reading for the bar to take Gandhi's place in South Africa, funded by Dr. Mehta.
updates.pjmehta: Pays for Sorabji's legal studies in London.
updates.jivraj: Takes part in planning the Indian volunteers.
updates.crewe: Accepts the Indian volunteers' offer after some hesitation.
updates.sarojini: First meeting: she has Gandhi's group sew soldiers' clothing.
updates.ww1: Gandhi rejects turning England's need into India's opportunity; about 80 Indians train for ambulance work.
updates.loyalty: Gandhi still believes the British system is tolerable and that officials can be won over by love.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has volunteered Indians for ambulance work in World War I, and friends are questioning it.
chapters.summary: Polak cables from South Africa asking how war service fits with ahimsa. Gandhi admits war can never be consistent with ahimsa, but argues that all living involves some violence. Since he enjoys the British Fleet's protection and is not yet able to resist war, he must either resist the Empire or serve it, and he chooses to serve. He makes no moral distinction between combatants and those who nurse them.

updates.gandhi: Defends his war service as a duty while admitting war contradicts ahimsa.
updates.polak: Cables to question how war service fits with Gandhi's ahimsa.
updates.hindswaraj: Gandhi had already discussed the morality of war in this book.
updates.ahimsa: No one is free of himsa, violence, simply by living. A votary of ahimsa should stop war, or, if unable to, may serve in it while striving to end it.
updates.ww1: Gandhi says nursing the wounded is as much participation in war as fighting.
updates.loyalty: His war service follows from his then-faith in the British connection.

chapters.situation: Gandhi's Indian ambulance corps is in training in London under a British commanding officer.
chapters.summary: Sorabji warns that the commanding officer means to lord it over them. The officer appoints Oxford students as section leaders and insists on full authority. Gandhi, laid up with pleurisy after drilling too soon after his fast, asks that the corps elect its own leaders, and the corps votes to stop drilling until they can. The officer divides the corps, but Under-Secretary Roberts proposes a compromise under which they serve at Netley Hospital answering only to its commander. Everyone goes except Gandhi, who is bedridden.

updates.gandhi: Leads a 'miniature satyagraha' from his sickbed over who commands the corps. Has pleurisy.
updates.sorabji: Warns Gandhi he is too trusting and jokes that satyagraha will be the death of them both.
updates.hobhouse: Had written that Gandhi might go to the gallows for truth.
updates.satyagraha: 'A Satyagrahi is born to be deceived… a deceiver only deceives himself.' The corps strikes over self-respect.
updates.ww1: Indian volunteers serve at Netley Hospital after a compromise.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is bedridden with pleurisy in London, and Gokhale has returned from Paris.
chapters.summary: Kallenbach shows Gokhale the war on the map. Dr. Jivraj Mehta and Gokhale press Gandhi to resume milk and cereals. After a sleepless night Gandhi decides to yield where his motives were mixed, but not on milk, which he gave up for religious reasons. Gokhale says he sees no religion in it but tells the doctor to treat Gandhi within his limits. Gokhale leaves London to escape the fogs.

updates.gandhi: Refuses milk, meat and milk products even under Gokhale's loving pressure.
updates.gokhale: Disapproves of Gandhi's fruit diet but stops pressing him out of affection, then leaves for India.
updates.jivraj: Treats Gandhi's pleurisy and urges milk, but has to work within Gandhi's limits.
updates.kallenbach: Explains the war to Gokhale on the map; supports whatever Gandhi decides.
updates.diet: Groundnuts, bananas, lemons, olive oil, tomatoes and grapes; no milk, cereals or pulses. The milk vow rests on religion and on the cruelty of Calcutta's dairymen.
updates.vows: Gandhi keeps a vow made for religious reasons and yields on choices made partly for health.
